## Welcome {#home}

### Hospital-Acquired Infections

**Learning Objectives:**

- Define hospital-acquired (nosocomial) infection
- Identify the four most common types of HAI
- Describe the source, route of spread, and recipient framework
- List standard precautions and device-specific prevention measures
- Distinguish barrier nursing from task nursing

🟢 **MUST KNOW** · 🟡 **SHOULD KNOW** · 🟣 **MAY KNOW** · 🧡 **QUESTION**

::: {.notes}
This module closes the disease-specific series by turning from
community transmission to the healthcare setting itself — the same
chain-of-infection framework from Chapter 6 applies, just with the
hospital as the environment.
:::

---

## Definition and Classification {background-color="#E3F2E1"}

🟢 **MUST KNOW**

A **hospital-acquired (nosocomial) infection** is one a patient develops
during treatment for another condition, **not present or incubating at
admission** — conventionally, onset **after 48 hours** of admission. It
can also affect healthcare workers.

The four most common types, each linked to an invasive device or
procedure:

| Type | Simplified criterion |
|---|---|
| **Urinary tract infection** | Positive culture, ≥10⁵ bacteria/mL |
| **Surgical site infection** | Purulent discharge/abscess/cellulitis within a month of surgery |
| **Respiratory infection** (esp. ventilator-associated pneumonia) | Respiratory symptoms + new infiltrate or purulent sputum |
| **Vascular catheter infection / septicaemia** | Inflammation at insertion site, or fever + positive blood culture |

---

## Source, Spread, and Recipient {background-color="#E3F2E1"}

🟢 **MUST KNOW**

HAIs are analyzed from three angles:

- **Source** — other patients, **hospital staff** (Staph aureus commonly
  carried in nose/skin; Salmonella in the gut), or the **environment**
  itself (hospital dust, surfaces)
- **Route of spread** — direct contact (most common: via hands),
  droplet, airborne particles, or contaminated equipment/procedures
  (catheterization, IV lines, dressings)
- **Recipient** — all patients are potential recipients, but risk is
  highest in the seriously ill, those on corticosteroids, and patients
  in ICU, urology, geriatric, or special newborn care units

---

## Prevention: Standard Precautions {background-color="#FFF6DA"}

🟡 **SHOULD KNOW**

Applied to the care of **every** patient, regardless of known infection
status:

- **Hand hygiene** — the single most important measure, since hands are
  the most common route of transmission; alcohol-based disinfectant when
  soap and water alone is insufficient
- **Personal protective equipment** — gloves for any contact risking
  contamination; gown, mask, and eye protection where splashing is
  anticipated
- **Sharps handled with extreme care**; hands washed immediately after
  glove removal
- **Isolation** of infectious patients; susceptible patients kept away
  from infection sources
- **Dust and droplet control** — wet dusting/vacuum cleaning (not dry
  sweeping), face masks, adequate bed spacing, ventilation

---

## Device-Specific Prevention {background-color="#FFF6DA"}

🟡 **SHOULD KNOW**

Evidence-based measures differ by infection type — knowing what
**doesn't** work is as important as what does:

| Infection | Proven effective | Proven NOT effective |
|---|---|---|
| **UTI** | Limiting catheter duration, aseptic insertion, closed drainage | Systemic antibiotic prophylaxis |
| **Surgical site** | Clean OR environment, optimal antibiotic timing, aseptic technique | Preoperative shaving, fumigation |
| **Ventilator pneumonia** | Aseptic suctioning, limiting ventilation duration | Routine ventilator-circuit changes every 48–72h |
| **Vascular catheter** | Closed system, limited duration, aseptic insertion | Antimicrobial skin creams |

---

## Nursing and Administrative Measures {background-color="#E8E4F3"}

🟣 **MAY KNOW**

| Approach | Focus | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| **Barrier nursing** | PPE, isolation, dedicated equipment, strict hand hygiene protocols | Prevent infection spread |
| **Task nursing** | Each staff member repeats specific duties across all patients, supervised by a head nurse | Efficient care delivery |

**Administrative control:** every hospital should have a **Control of
Infection Committee** — responsible for policies on admission of
infectious cases, isolation facilities, disinfection procedures, and
overall HAI surveillance and response.

## Self-Check: Question 1 {background-color="#FDE8E8"}

🧡 **QUESTION**

::: {.quiz-question}
### Question 1

By convention, an infection is classified as hospital-acquired
(nosocomial) if it becomes apparent:

- Within 24 hours of admission
- [After 48 hours of admission, and not present or incubating at admission]{.correct data-explanation="The standard definition requires onset after 48 hours of admission, distinguishing it from a community-acquired infection the patient already had or was incubating on arrival."}
- Only after discharge
- Only in ICU patients
:::

## Self-Check: Question 2 {background-color="#FDE8E8"}

🧡 **QUESTION**

::: {.quiz-question}
### Question 2

The single most important and most common route of transmission for
hospital-acquired infections is:

- Airborne particles
- Contaminated hospital dust
- [Direct contact via the hands of healthcare workers]{.correct data-explanation="Hand contact is the most common route of cross-infection in hospitals, which is why hand hygiene is the cornerstone of standard precautions."}
- Contaminated food
:::

## Self-Check: Question 3 {background-color="#FDE8E8"}

🧡 **QUESTION**

::: {.quiz-question}
### Question 3

Which of the following is a proven-**ineffective** measure for
preventing catheter-associated urinary tract infection?

- Limiting catheter duration
- Aseptic technique at insertion
- Maintaining closed drainage
- [Systemic antibiotic prophylaxis]{.correct data-explanation="Systemic antibiotic prophylaxis has not been shown to be effective for preventing catheter-associated UTIs and is not recommended; catheter-duration limitation and aseptic technique are the proven measures."}
:::
